title: A stroke, and the setup
goal: Know exactly what a stroke is in the generator (24 bits plus one spelling bit), which data sources feed every pronunciation, and how the IPA fallback turns a pronunciation the main dictionary lacks into one the rules can read.

blocks.x: A stroke is one u32

The generator in `src/generate/` turns a word list into a stroke for every word. Everything it does (candidate generation, the cost function, the solver, phrase merges) works on a single bit pattern per stroke. There is no struct of "which keys are down": the bits are the keys.

blocks.x: The first five regions are the 22 physical steno keys; `+` and `~` are lyk's own markers, checked the same way as every other bit. A stroke with only `+` or only `~` set is not a stroke.
Onset and coda consonants are different bits even when they are the same letter. The right bank's `T` (coda t) and the left bank's `T` (onset t) never collide.
Worked bit example
[[cat|KAT]] is K (left bank) + A (left vowel) + T (right bank): three bits set out of twenty-four, every other region zero.

blocks.x: Setup: six sources loaded in parallel

`Setup::load` (in `src/analysis/mod.rs`) loads six independent sources on their own threads, then merges the pronunciation sources by strict priority, not as a union. The whole load takes about half a second.

Role
rows: Word counts and rank. Names are counted at a tenth (see below).
The briefs kept as candidates, and which words are written only capitalized (names).
Word-pair counts for phrase merging, kept only for words that are ranked.

blocks.x: CMUdict first. Only where CMUdict has no entry at all does a translated MFA or WikiPron pronunciation get a chance; a CMUdict word is never touched.
Contractions the frequency list spells without an apostrophe

The frequency list counts some contractions under their apostrophe-stripped spelling (`dont`, `cant`, `didnt`). If CMUdict has a real pronunciation for the apostrophe form and the list does not carry it, the apostrophe form is inserted directly after the stripped one with the same count.
Names count a tenth

Subtitles say names constantly (435 of the 5,000 commonest words in the current build). A word that Plover and Lapwing only ever write capitalized is a name, and its count is divided by ten (rounded up, so a name said once is still said). The effect: a name never outranks the word it sounds like. [[mat|PHAT]] holds `PHAT`; the name Matt types as its sound-alike after the capitalize stroke `KPA` (see [Phrases and capitals](#/ref/punctuation)).
The IPA fallback in four steps

MFA and WikiPron record pronunciation as IPA, not ARPAbet, and in two different IPA conventions. `src/ipa.rs` translates either into the 39-symbol ARPAbet alphabet CMUdict uses. Roughly 8,000 words with no CMUdict entry are rescued this way in the current build.

head: Step
What it does
rows: Strip non-distinctive modifiers: aspiration `ʰ`, palatalization `ʲ`, length `ː`, tie bars. A syllabic-consonant mark is flagged separately so it can expand into an inserted schwa.
WikiPron splits one diphthong across two vowel tokens (`b a ʊ t` for bout); MFA writes it as one (`!aw`). Both collapse to a single phone before anything is looked up.
Every remaining token goes through a consonant, vowel or diphthong table. One unrecognized symbol fails the whole pronunciation: no partial, guessed translation ever ships.
Neither source marks lexical stress. The first vowel becomes primary (`1`), every other vowel unstressed (`0`). This is often wrong for a later-stressed word such as began.

blocks.x: Step 4 is a known limitation: the fallback guesses stress from position, so a word whose stress falls later can be split into syllables the wrong way. A word with no pronunciation at all gets no outline from the rules; it can still be spelled letter by letter (see [Spelling mode](#/ref/spelling-mode)).
